passage:
By Thursday afternoon at the ad agency in Andheri, Kashish had built a whole story. Sachin hadn't laughed at her joke in the stand-up. He'd answered her draft with "noted." He'd eaten lunch at his desk instead of joining them.

He thinks I stole the tea-brand pitch idea, she thought. He's going to say it in Monday's review. She'd already rehearsed three replies in the washroom mirror.

At four she caught herself drafting a fourth. Enough. She walked over to his desk.

"Sachin, can I ask something? Are you annoyed with me about the pitch? I'd rather ask than keep guessing."

He looked up, surprised. "What? No! My landlord's selling the flat and I have to move by the fifteenth. I've been apartment-hunting on my phone all day. Sorry, I've been a zombie."

The whole thing took two minutes. Kashish went back to her desk and deleted the fourth reply.

qa.q: What did Sachin answer Kashish's draft with?
qa.a: He'd answered her draft with "noted."

qa.q: Why did Kashish's story about Sachin feel so convincing to her?
qa.a: Each small sign, the missed laugh, the short reply and the lunch at his desk, seemed to fit one explanation. Rehearsing replies in the mirror made the imagined conflict feel even more real.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work so quickly?
qa.a: Kashish caught herself drafting a fourth reply and decided to ask Sachin directly. One two-minute question replaced days of guessing with his actual reason.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Kashish asked if he was annoyed?
qa.a: Sachin was surprised, and maybe a little relieved to explain why he'd been so distracted. He might also have felt bad that his stress had come across as coldness.

Tea break at the tea estate office, Darjeeling. Dolma waited until the others had gone out to the verandah.

"Anirban-da, do you have a minute?"

"Hmm?" He didn't look up from the ledger.

"You've been very quiet with me since Tuesday. You didn't come to see the new drying racks with me. I've been wondering if I did something."

He looked up. "You? No."

"I thought maybe the racks report. I changed your figures."

"You fixed them. I was glad." He rubbed his eyes. "My mother's been unwell. I've been at the hospital at night. I'm not with anyone, Dolma. I'm barely here."

"Oh." Dolma sat down. "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head."

He almost smiled. "Did I win?"

"Every time." She pushed her cup towards him. "Drink this. I'll show you the racks tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Dolma think Anirban might be upset about?
qa.a: The racks report, where she changed his figures.

qa.q: What does "I've spent three days writing arguments with you in my head" show about Dolma's state before she asked?
qa.a: It shows she was anxious and sure she had upset him, building imagined conflicts for days. Her guess felt real enough to argue with.

qa.q: Which choice of Dolma's made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Waiting until they were alone and asking plainly whether she had done something. It gave Anirban the chance to tell her the real reason in a minute.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel after Dolma asks him directly?
qa.a: Anirban may feel relieved to share what's going on with his mother, and touched that Dolma cared enough to ask. His small joke suggests some of the weight lifted.

passage:
At the primary school in a village near Bijapur, Yusuf had been sure since morning that Sangeeta was annoyed with him. She hadn't returned his "namaste" at the gate. She'd walked past his classroom without looking in. At lunch she sat at the far end of the verandah.

By two o'clock Yusuf had built a whole case in his head. It must be the mid-day meal register he'd filled in late on Monday. She'd complain to the block officer. She'd say, "Yusuf sir is careless," in the next meeting.

At three, instead of stewing through the last period, he walked over. "Sangeeta ma'am, is something wrong? Did I upset you?"

She looked up, surprised, a hand pressed to her cheek. "Upset? No, Yusuf sir. I've had a toothache since last night. I can barely see straight."

Yusuf laughed at himself all the way home.

qa.a: It replaced hours of imagined complaints and meetings with the simple truth: a toothache.

passage:
In the Stockholm office, Ingrid presented her new schedule for the team, and Alejandro, who usually had a joke for everything, said only, "Fine," and looked at his laptop.

All afternoon Ingrid replayed it. He thinks it's a bad plan. He thinks I'm bossy because I'm new. He'll tell the others it won't work. By four o'clock she had drafted, in her head, a whole argument defending the schedule.

Then she remembered what her old manager used to say: "Check the story before you believe it."

She walked to his desk. "Alejandro, quick question. When I showed the schedule, you seemed quiet. Is something about it a problem? I'd rather hear it than guess."

He looked up, surprised. "The schedule? No, it's good. My daughter's sick at home. I've been checking my phone all day."

"Oh, I'm sorry. Go home if you need to."

He smiled. "Thanks. And thanks for asking."
